questions.q: What is the grain of a transaction fact table like f_SalesOrderLine?
options: One row per sales order line
One row per customer per year
One row per warehouse per day
One row per product, regardless of how many times it was sold
questions.explain: A transaction fact table records one row per business event — in this example, one row per line item on a sales order.

questions.q: Why doesn't the f_SalesOrderLine example include a formal primary key?
options: The row is already identified well enough by its dimension keys and attributes, and a primary key would add storage overhead a billion-row table can't afford
SQL Server does not support primary keys on fact tables
Fact tables are not allowed to have any keys at all
Primary keys are only used on dimension tables, never fact tables
questions.explain: Microsoft's own reference fact table structure omits a primary key for exactly this reason — it rarely serves a useful purpose and costs storage at scale.

questions.q: In the f_SalesOrderLine example, what role do SalesOrderNo and SalesOrderLineNo play?
options: They are attributes that help set the grain, not dimension keys or measures
They are the table's measures, summed to compute total revenue
They are foreign keys to a Date dimension
They are audit columns tracking who loaded the row
questions.explain: Columns like an order number set the table's grain without joining to a dimension table — that makes them attributes, specifically a degenerate dimension, covered properly in Chapter 3.

questions.q: Why are transaction fact table measures like LineRevenue typically fully additive?
options: Because each row represents a genuinely independent business event, so summing across any combination of dimensions produces a meaningful total
Because SQL Server automatically converts every measure to be additive
Because transaction fact tables never contain more than one measure
Additive just means the column data type is INT
questions.explain: Independent events can be safely summed across products, customers, dates, or any other dimension — that's the practical payoff of getting a transaction fact table's grain right.

questions.q: You're about to add a PromotionCode column to a sales-order-line fact table, but the promotion actually applies once per whole order, not per line. What's the problem?
options: It violates the declared grain — every column in a fact table must be true at the grain of one row, and a per-order value isn't true at the per-line grain
There is no problem — any column can be added to any fact table
PromotionCode should be stored as a measure instead of an attribute
The column would need to be renamed to PromotionCode_FK to work correctly
questions.explain: Deciding the grain first (Lesson 4) means every column has to hold true at that grain — a per-order fact doesn't belong on a per-line row without changing the design.
